The estuary seahorse Hippocampus kuda exhibits a life history characterized by a relatively rapid early growth trajectory and a modest final body size. Females transfer their oocytes into the male's brood pouch during a spawning event, where internal fertilization and subsequent male pregnancy occur. The newly released juveniles, or yolk-sac fry, emerge from the pouch after a developmental period of approximately 24 days [ab = approximately 24 days] when the water temperature is maintained at 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. Upon birth, these neonatal individuals have a remarkably low wet weight of about 0.0031 grams [Wwb = about 0.0031 grams], one of the smallest birth masses recorded among syngnathids, reflecting the limited yolk reserves provided by the male brood pouch.

As juveniles grow and develop within seagrass and mangrove habitats, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic expansion before reaching the threshold of sexual maturation. A study of wild-caught specimens from a Philippine estuary established that the total length at which 50% of individuals attain puberty is 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm]. Corresponding morphometric data indicated that the wet weight associated with this pubertal stage is 11.7 grams [Wwp = 11.7 grams]. These values, derived from field surveys, place Hippocampus kuda among the medium-sized members of its genus, with a body plan that remains slender throughout the sub-adult phase.

The time required for a newborn individual to reach the pubertal milestone has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions. At a constant water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], the interval from birth to the onset of gonadal development is approximately 98 days [tp = approximately 98 days]. This period of rapid mass gain and skeletal ossification allows the juvenile to attain the critical size necessary for the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Following this pubertal event, the seahorse continues to grow, eventually approaching its ultimate size after several additional months of feeding on copepods and small crustaceans.

Once maturity is reached, the maximum recorded total length for the estuary seahorse is 30 cm [Li = 30 cm]. At this asymptotic size, an adult individual attains a wet weight of 115 grams [Wwi = 115 grams], representing a more than 37,000-fold increase from the neonatal mass. This impressive growth trajectory is sustained by a high rate of prey capture. In terms of reproductive output, a single male can brood approximately 1000 offspring per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately 1000 offspring per reproductive event], with about 2.7 broods per year [F_R_i = about 2.7 broods per year] when maintained at 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], a rate that reflects the continuous brooding strategy characteristic of male-pregnant syngnathids.

The lifespan of Hippocampus kuda in natural settings is constrained by predation and environmental fluctuations, yet captive studies provide a clearer picture of its physiological longevity. The maximum documented lifespan for this species is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under stable aquarium conditions at 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. This relatively extended duration, combined with its iteroparous breeding strategy, allows for multiple reproductive cycles across the adult phase. The species' moderate growth rate and delayed senescence are consistent with life-history patterns observed in other seahorses inhabiting shallow tropical estuaries, where resource availability is seasonally variable.
